title: Measures
hookLine: character traits are called middot, measures, meant to be set at the right amount

cards: A pinch of salt makes the bread. A cup of salt ruins it. Nobody in the kitchen calls salt good or bad; the only question anyone asks is how much.
Hebrew talks about a person's character the way a cook talks about salt.
The word for a trait, like patience or generosity or courage, is the word for a measure: something you can have too little of, too much of, or just the right amount.

teach.h: THE SAME WORD KEEPS THE SCALE HONEST.
teach.b: Middot. One trait is a middah, a measure; many traits are middot. Four turns.
First, the marketplace. Leviticus forbids cheating in judgment, in length, in weight, or in measure, and the Hebrew word there for the measure of length is middah.
The word that keeps a merchant's yardstick honest is the word Jewish teachers use for character: something checked against a standard, like a scale. Second, the middle.

teach.h: MOST TRAITS LIVE BETWEEN TWO ENDS.
teach.b: Maimonides, in his laws about character traits, sets each trait between two extremes. Take anger. At one end, the person who flares at everything.
At the other, a person so numb nothing moves them, like the dead, he says. The wise, he teaches, usually keep the measure in between. Third, the exceptions.

teach.h: PRIDE AND ANGER: GO PAST THE MIDDLE.
teach.b: For pride and for anger, Maimonides advised going well past the middle, toward humility and calm, because those two do so much damage. A measure isn't always halfway. Fourth, the highest use.
Jewish prayer calls the qualities God reveals to Moses in Exodus, merciful and gracious, slow to anger, the middot of mercy. The same word names God's ways and a person's habits.
So when a Mussar teacher says work on your middot, the picture isn't good traits versus bad ones. It's a set of dials. Too little patience, and you snap; too much, and you let a wrong go on.
Too little generosity, and your hand stays closed; too much, and your own family goes without. The work is turning each dial toward its right setting, a little at a time.

how: In Mussar study groups, Jews often pick one middah, such as patience or generosity, study texts about it, and watch for it in their own week, aiming for its right measure rather than its extreme.

games.q: you're Maimonides, writing about anger. where do you set the right measure?
o: exactly halfway, like every other trait.
well past the middle, toward calm.
anywhere, as long as you mean well.
games.why: for most traits he points to the middle, but for anger, and for pride, he advises going well past it, toward calm and humility.

practice: Take the trait you chose yesterday, or any that comes to mind, and picture a line: too little of it at one end, too much at the other.
Place yourself on that line as you were this past week, not where you hope or fear you are, and notice one moment that shows it, and which way the dial might turn.
If you pray, bring this to God in your own words; if not, keep the picture of the line in view.

wordCard.voice: Middot. Measures: the Hebrew word for character traits, the Torah's word for an honest measure in the market, each set at its right amount. Today's word.
